title: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 6 — Write Like Crazy
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that the Common Core's call for frequent writing (W.CCR.10) is one of the highest-leverage standards because writing simultaneously builds reading comprehension, content mastery and thinking. He grounds the claim in the Writing to Read meta-analysis and in studies linking writing to gains in math and science achievement. His practical core is to pair every reading task with a short written response built on teacher-made inferential or argumentative prompts rather than textbook end-of-chapter questions. He then answers the workload objection head-on, borrowing Kelly Gallagher's practice of reading only a fraction of student writing and Mike Schmoker's 'write more, grade less' techniques. Finally, he insists that extended papers still matter, offering benchmarks for content-area and English classes while reminding content teachers to aim at clarity, content and evidence rather than literary polish.
points: Tying every reading assignment to a brief written response, prompted by teacher-made questions about inference, argument or significance, is presented as the simplest route to serious literacy gains.
Stuart warns that textbook end-of-section questions are typically low- to zero-effective because they are written by people who have never taught.
Teachers can sustain high writing volume without burning out by reading only about one in four informal pieces, as Kelly Gallagher does, while students never know which piece will be read.
Extended papers remain essential: one to two a year in content areas and up to one a month in English, with most of the work done in class under teacher supervision.
Content-area teachers should aim for clarity, content and evidence-based citation, leaving the finer points of style to ELA colleagues.
quotes: One of the biggest bang-for-your-buck Common Core standards is W.CCR.10, which basically says, “Write frequently for many reasons.” And the amazing thing about writing is that it achieves so many things simultaneously.

One thing I would say not to do is simply tell kids to read Chapter 13, Section 2, and answer all of the questions at the back of the book. The questions and activities provided with textbooks are often designed by people who have never taught, and they are generally low- to zero-effective in helping kids become better readers, writers, and thinkers.

Instead, create your own response questions that are interesting and simple; these questions, like the examples above, should be along the lines of reading between the lines (inferring), arguing, making connections to other content, or drawing conclusions.

If you just do this — add writing to every reading task — and if you give kids one to two opportunities minimum to read complex texts every week, I'd be shocked not to see some serious gains in your kids in the areas of reading and writing.
He went on to say that his students never know which of their pieces he's going to read, so they stay on their toes while he stays sane.
The length of these papers should increase with each grade level, and the bulk of the work should be done in class so we can walk around checking for understanding and ensuring student success.

The key for content area teachers is to remember that we are not English teachers — we're aiming for clarity and content, as Mike Schmoker says, as well as the ability to cite written sources to support arguments or conclusions with evidence.
